H-CHICKEN-D.text: There’s a chicken-and-egg dilemma here. You may be so deep in your child-state that you can’t become the adult you need, yet offering yourself love is easier when you already have access to at least one of your adult roles. What happens when that access is missing? You might try saying loving words while the inherited critic, numbness, panic, or the urge to escape dominates the process. You’re trying to offer the love you need, but the difficulty of accessing the adult who could provide it leaves the attempt uncertain.

H-CHICKEN-E.text: Giving yourself love is easier when you can already access at least one of your adult roles. That creates a chicken-and-egg dilemma: you may be so deep in your child-state that you can’t become the adult you need. You might try saying loving words while the inherited critic, numbness, panic, or the urge to escape still dominates the process. The words may be loving, but without access to that adult role, it’s uncertain whether you can offer the love you’re trying to give.

H-SOM-E.text:
You can know that the danger is over and that you are safe while your body continues to react: trauma reactions may persist beyond the objective threat, and conscious knowledge does not necessarily shift that bodily state. With complex or developmental trauma, going straight to the deepest memory can overwhelm someone, so gentle, gradual work around the edges may suffice. Buddhist nun Pema Chodron uses the phrase “feather touch” for a gentle approach; Peter Levine, founder of Somatic Experiencing, calls gentle work around the edges “pendulation.”

A parallel arises in inner-child therapy, where knowing what is needed does not always mean being able to provide it. You may understand what the younger part needs yet become so absorbed in the child-state that you have too little access to an adult perspective to meet those needs.

H-SOM-D.text:
The danger is over. You know you’re safe. Yet your body’s trauma reactions may persist, because conscious knowledge of safety does not necessarily shift your bodily state. With complex or developmental trauma, going straight to the deepest memory can overwhelm you; gentle, gradual work around the edges may suffice. Buddhist nun Pema Chodron uses the phrase “feather touch” for a gentle approach, while Peter Levine, founder of Somatic Experiencing, calls gentle work around the edges “pendulation.”

There’s a parallel in inner-child therapy: you may know what the younger part needs but be so absorbed in the child-state that you don’t have enough access to your adult perspective to offer it. Knowing what’s needed and being able to provide it are separate things.
